summary: Describes using elliptic curve algorithms, ECDH with EnvelopedData and ECDSA with SignedData, for the CMS encrypted key package content type. It extends RFC 6033 and is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Says how to use a compact kind of math lock and signature when sending a box that holds secret keys.

subtitle: Adds elliptic curve ECDH and ECDSA as options for protecting encrypted key packages in CMS.

tldr.problem: RFC 6033 lists algorithms for the CMS encrypted key package content type, but it did not cover Elliptic Curve algorithms.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6161 says implementations MAY support standard ECDH with EnvelopedData and ECDSA with SignedData, and MUST support keys on the P-256 curve if they support either.
tldr.outcome: It defines no new algorithms. It only points to existing ones and extends RFC 6033; it is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 6161 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 6033. No later RFC obsoletes it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 6161 describes conventions for using Elliptic Curve cryptographic algorithms with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) encrypted key package content type from RFC 6032. It covers two CMS content types, EnvelopedData and SignedData, and amends RFC 6033.

The document does not define any new algorithms. It refers to previously defined ones, and readers are assumed to be familiar with RFC 6033 and RFC 5753.
sections.eli5: This note adds two more allowed tools for protecting a package of keys. It does not invent new tools, it just points to ones that already exist.

sections.title: ECDH and ECDSA Choices
sections.content:
For EnvelopedData, when key agreement is used, standard (as opposed to cofactor) Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) MAY be supported. The algorithms are those in RFC 6090 and RFC 5753.

For SignedData, an implementation that encapsulates EncryptedKeyPackage with SignedData MAY support the signature scheme Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA). Both are optional: the words are MAY, not MUST.
sections.eli5: ECDH is a way for two people to agree on a secret lock key without sharing it openly. ECDSA is a way to sign the box so people know who sent it. Both are allowed, but nobody is forced to use them.

sections.title: Public Key Sizes
sections.content:
The easiest way to implement SignedData and EnvelopedData is with public key certificates, as profiled in RFC 5280 and RFC 5480.

If an implementation supports ECDSA or ECDH, then it MUST support keys on the P-256 curve. That gives everyone one curve they can rely on.
sections.eli5: If you choose to use these tools, you must at least know one standard size of key, so that everyone can understand each other.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document adds no security text of its own. It says the security considerations from RFC 5280, RFC 5480, RFC 5652, RFC 5753, RFC 6033 and RFC 6090 apply.
sections.eli5: The safety rules are the ones already written in the older documents, and they still count.
